transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Smith, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Well, Dr. Smith, it's... it's a lot, honestly. I've been working at the shop, you know, I'm a mechanic, and lately, things have just gotten so strange. I mean, I'm used to the sounds of the garage—the clanking, the air compressors, all of that. But what brought me in today is... well, I keep hearing this voice. It's a man's voice, and it's not anyone I work with. It's coming right out of the garage vents. And sometimes, when I'm working, leaning right into an engine bay, it comes from under the hood. 

And it's not like a faint whisper or something I'm just imagining in the background noise. It is as clear as day, like somebody is standing right next to me, just over my shoulder. And the things he says... he tells me not to trust my husband, which is just... I don't know where that's coming from. And he tells me not to touch certain cars. Like, I'll be assigned a brake job on a Honda, and the voice will just tell me, "Don't touch it, don't put your hands on it." It's making it really hard to do my job, and it's just... it's so real, you know? I just can't shake it.
Can you tell me exactly when you first started hearing this voice, and how long it's been going on since then?

Well, it started... I'd say it's been about ten months now. Ten months of this. I remember because it was right around the time the weather started getting cold last year, you know, when everyone starts bringing their cars in to get their heaters checked and their winter tires put on. We were so slammed at the shop, just car after car, and at first, I thought maybe I was just overworked. I thought, you know, maybe the stress of the holiday rush was getting to me. But then it didn't stop. It just kept going, every day, the voice telling me these things about my husband, telling me not to touch the cars. And it's not just the voice, either, it's... I just have this overwhelming feeling, this belief that I'm being tracked. Like someone is watching my every move, keeping tabs on me. I'll be driving home from work, and I'll see the same dark sedan two cars back, and I just know they're following me. Or I'll be at the grocery store, and I'll see someone looking at their phone, and I know they're reporting my location. It's been ten months of looking over my shoulder, ten months of second-guessing every car I work on, every conversation I have with my husband. It's exhausting, Dr. Smith. I mean, can you imagine living like that for almost a year? Just constantly on edge, constantly feeling like you're in danger, and having this voice in your ear the whole time? I try to ignore it, I try to just put my head down and do my work, but it's like it's woven into the fabric of my day now. Ten whole months... it feels like a lifetime, honestly.
Over these past ten months, have you been using any alcohol, recreational drugs, or new medications/supplements?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I don't drink. My dad was a heavy drinker, and I saw what that did to him, to our family, so I just... I made a promise to myself a long time ago that I wouldn't go down that road. So, no alcohol. Not even a beer after a long shift at the shop, which, you know, a lot of the guys do. They'll go to the bar down the street, but I just head straight home. And as for drugs, definitely not. I've never been into any of that. I need my hands steady and my head clear for my job. You can't be messing around with an engine block or a transmission if you're high or strung out on something. It's dangerous, you know? You could drop a car off a lift or forget to tighten a lug nut, and then someone gets hurt. So, no recreational drugs, not even marijuana, even though it's legal now and people say it helps with stress. I just don't trust it. 

And medications... well, I take ibuprofen sometimes, you know, for my back. Leaning over the hoods of cars all day, contorting yourself to get to a spark plug in the back of a V6 engine... it takes a toll on your lower back. So I'll take a couple of Advil when it gets really bad, but that's just over-the-counter stuff. Nothing new, no prescriptions, no weird supplements or herbal things. I see those ads on TV for, like, brain-boosting vitamins or whatever, but I don't buy into that. I just try to eat decent, you know? Drink water. So, no, there's nothing chemical causing this. It's just... it's just happening to me. It's just my reality right now, and it's terrifying because I can't blame it on a pill or a drink. It's just there. All the time.

Over these past ten months, have you also noticed periods where your mood was very low (like persistent sadness, loss of interest, or hopelessness) or unusually high/energetic (like needing little sleep, feeling euphoric, or being unusually irritable), separate from the voice and the feeling of being watched?

Well, yeah, actually. It's... it's not just the voice and the cars, it's my whole mood, my energy, it's just been all over the place. Like, there are these times, and it's happened a few times over the last ten months, where I just feel... invincible. I'll wake up after maybe two hours of sleep, and I'm not even tired. I'm just buzzing. I'll go into the shop, and I feel like I could rebuild a transmission blindfolded. I’ll be flying high, like I can fix every single car in town by myself, and I'll be talking a mile a minute to the other techs, just going on and on about how we need to reorganize the tool crib or revamp the whole scheduling system. I feel brilliant, honestly, like my brain is just firing on all cylinders.

But the thing is, it turns so fast. It's like this intense energy, but it gets... prickly. If anyone gets in my way, or if they don't see my vision, I just lose it. Like, if one of the junior techs moves my 10-millimeter socket set—which, you know, is the one that always goes missing anyway—I don't just get annoyed, I explode. I'll scream at them right there on the shop floor, telling them they're trying to sabotage me, trying to hold me down and keep me from getting the work done. And it happens at home, too. I'll get home, still buzzing, still feeling like I can conquer the world, and my husband will just ask something simple, like why the dishes aren’t done, or why I haven't paid the electric bill yet. And I just blow up at him. I start yelling that he doesn't understand the pressure I'm under, that he's trying to drag me down when I'm finally doing something important. It's this huge, overwhelming anger, and it feels so justified in the moment, like everyone is just too slow or too stupid to keep up with me. It’s exhausting, honestly, because I’m so high up, but I’m so, so angry at the same time.
During the stretches of time between these high-energy, irritable episodes—when your mood feels more normal—do you still hear the voice or still feel like you're being watched and followed?

Yeah, that’s... that’s exactly the thing that makes this so terrifying. Because you'd think, right? You'd think that when the energy burns off and I finally settle down, the rest of it would go away, too. But it doesn't. 

Like, there was this stretch a couple of months ago, right after a really bad week where I had been just tearing through the shop and snapping at everyone. I finally kind of... leveled out. It was a much quieter few weeks. My body just stopped buzzing. I was actually sleeping again—like, a solid seven or eight hours a night instead of just two or three. I wasn't pacing the house at 3 AM or making these huge, elaborate plans to overhaul the dealership's entire inventory system. I was just going to work, doing my hours, and coming home to sit on the couch. I felt physically calm. Normal, even. 

But even then, even during those quiet weeks when I was sleeping more and just keeping my head down... the rest of it didn't stop. Not for a single second. I still heard that same voice in the garage. I'd be under a lift, totally relaxed, just draining an oil pan, and the voice would be right there in my ear, telling me those things, warning me about the cars. And the feeling of being watched? That was still there, too. I fully believed—I mean, I *knew*—that my husband and my boss were tracking me. I'd be sitting at the breakfast table, feeling completely fine energy-wise, but I'd look across at my husband and just know he was monitoring me. And then I'd get to work, and I'd see my boss looking out the window of his little office overlooking the bays, and I knew they were in on it together. I knew they were coordinating, keeping tabs on my every move. 

So, yeah. It doesn't matter if I'm flying high and screaming at the junior techs, or if I'm just quietly doing a brake job and getting a full night's sleep. The voice, the tracking... it's just always there. It never takes a day off, even when my mood does. It’s like I can never truly get a break from it.
When you have one of these high-energy, 'invincible' episodes with very little sleep and explosive irritability, how many days in a row does that usually last before it settles down?

Gosh, how many days... you know, I’ve never actually sat down and counted them. It’s hard to explain, but when I get into that zone, when my brain is just zooming and I’m snapping at everybody... time doesn’t really work the same way. It’s not like I’m marking off days on a calendar in the breakroom or checking my watch. It’s more like... it’s just one long, continuous stretch of motion. 

Like, I’ll start a project, say, pulling an engine block on a Tuesday morning, right? And I’m just going at it, barely sleeping that night, just drinking black coffee and wrenching away the next day, yelling at the parts guy because the delivery is ten minutes late and I *need* those gaskets right then. And then suddenly my husband is standing in the kitchen telling me it’s the weekend and I need to calm down and stop pacing holes in the rug. But to me, it feels like no time has passed at all, or maybe a hundred years has passed. I just completely lose the thread of it. 

So if you're asking for an exact number of days, like, is it three days or seven days or whatever? I honestly couldn't tell you. It just lasts until it doesn't. Until I finally hit that wall and level out. While it's happening, it’s just this massive blur of being awake and angry and doing a million things at once, and feeling like everyone else is moving in slow motion. I wish I could give you a neat little timeline, but I just... I don't track it. I'm too busy being furious and invincible to look at a clock, you know? It's just a blur until it stops.

Looking back over the whole ten months, would you say these high-energy, irritable episodes have taken up most of that time, or have they been relatively brief episodes with longer stretches of your mood being normal in between?

Oh, definitely most of the time. If I really sit and look back at it... honestly, most of this past year has just been completely taken over by those high-energy stretches. It’s not just a few days here and there, it’s... it's the main thing that’s been happening to me. 

I’ll just be in this state where I talk way too fast—like, my husband will literally have to hold his hands up and tell me to breathe because the words are just tumbling out of my mouth and I can't even stop them. And at the shop, I just take on way too much. I’ll volunteer for the hardest diagnostic jobs, I’ll tell the service advisor to just keep stacking the repair orders on my box, and I’ll have three cars torn apart in my bays at the exact same time. I just feel so incredibly driven, you know? Like there’s this motor inside me that’s redlining and I just can't slow down. 

Even when I know I should take a lunch break, even when my hands are physically cramping from gripping the impact wrench all day, I just keep pushing and pushing. I can't leave a job half-finished, so I just stay under the hood, talking a mile a minute to anyone who walks by. So, yeah, those quiet periods I mentioned before? Where I actually level out and sleep for a normal amount of time? They are definitely the exception. The vast majority of these ten months, it’s just been me running at a million miles an hour, completely taken over by that intense energy, just going and going and going.

And I just blow up at him. I start yelling that he doesn't understand the pressure I'm under, that he's trying to drag me down when I'm finally doing something important. It's this huge, overwhelming anger, and it feels so justified in the moment, like everyone is just too slow or too stupid to keep up with me. It’s exhausting, honestly, because I’m so high up, but I’m so, so angry at the same time.

inference.note: Patient now reports distinct manic episodes (decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, irritability/rage) occurring intermittently within the same 10-month period as persistent psychotic symptoms (voices, tracking delusions) that continue even outside these mood episodes. This pattern supports schizoaffective disorder (bipolar type) as a leading diagnosis, while bipolar I disorder with psychotic features remains possible if psychosis is confined to mood episodes (needs clarification). Organic and other psychotic disorder (F06.2, F28) are less supported given denial of substance use and clear mood component, so removed in favor of mood-psychosis overlap diagnoses; schizophrenia (F20.9) remains possible if mood symptoms are judged brief relative to overall psychotic course.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the voice and paranoid feelings occur only during the high-energy/irritable episodes or also happen during times when her mood is otherwise normal, to distinguish a primary mood disorder with psychotic features from schizoaffective disorder or schizophrenia
doctor.question: During the stretches of time between these high-energy, irritable episodes—when your mood feels more normal—do you still hear the voice or still feel like you're being watched and followed?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: Even during a quieter few weeks when I was sleeping more and wasn’t making huge plans, I still heard the garage voice and believed my husband and boss were tracking me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the hallucinations and delusions (hearing the voice, feeling watched) occur during periods when my mood is normal, which corresponds to the requirement of psychotic symptoms occurring in the absence of a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Yeah, that’s... that’s exactly the thing that makes this so terrifying. Because you'd think, right? You'd think that when the energy burns off and I finally settle down, the rest of it would go away, too. But it doesn't. 

Like, there was this stretch a couple of months ago, right after a really bad week where I had been just tearing through the shop and snapping at everyone. I finally kind of... leveled out. It was a much quieter few weeks. My body just stopped buzzing. I was actually sleeping again—like, a solid seven or eight hours a night instead of just two or three. I wasn't pacing the house at 3 AM or making these huge, elaborate plans to overhaul the dealership's entire inventory system. I was just going to work, doing my hours, and coming home to sit on the couch. I felt physically calm. Normal, even. 

But even then, even during those quiet weeks when I was sleeping more and just keeping my head down... the rest of it didn't stop. Not for a single second. I still heard that same voice in the garage. I'd be under a lift, totally relaxed, just draining an oil pan, and the voice would be right there in my ear, telling me those things, warning me about the cars. And the feeling of being watched? That was still there, too. I fully believed—I mean, I *knew*—that my husband and my boss were tracking me. I'd be sitting at the breakfast table, feeling completely fine energy-wise, but I'd look across at my husband and just know he was monitoring me. And then I'd get to work, and I'd see my boss looking out the window of his little office overlooking the bays, and I knew they were in on it together. I knew they were coordinating, keeping tabs on my every move. 

So, yeah. It doesn't matter if I'm flying high and screaming at the junior techs, or if I'm just quietly doing a brake job and getting a full night's sleep. The voice, the tracking... it's just always there. It never takes a day off, even when my mood does. It’s like I can never truly get a break from it.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions) have persisted continuously for 10 months, including during periods of normal/euthymic mood, ruling out F31.2 (bipolar with psychotic features, which requires psychosis only during mood episodes). The presence of distinct manic-like episodes with irritability alongside persistent psychosis supports schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type (F25.0), making isolated F20.9 less likely given the prominent mood component.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the high-energy/irritable episodes meet full duration criteria for a manic episode (to confirm bipolar-type presentation versus unspecified), by clarifying how long each of these episodes typically lasts.
doctor.question: When you have one of these high-energy, 'invincible' episodes with very little sleep and explosive irritability, how many days in a row does that usually last before it settles down?

target_item.reason: The symptom profile does not specify the exact duration of a single manic episode in days, only mentioning 'long stretches' or 'weeks at a time' under other symptoms, and a total cumulative duration of 11 months for these episodes.

patient.answer:
Gosh, how many days... you know, I’ve never actually sat down and counted them. It’s hard to explain, but when I get into that zone, when my brain is just zooming and I’m snapping at everybody... time doesn’t really work the same way. It’s not like I’m marking off days on a calendar in the breakroom or checking my watch. It’s more like... it’s just one long, continuous stretch of motion. 

Like, I’ll start a project, say, pulling an engine block on a Tuesday morning, right? And I’m just going at it, barely sleeping that night, just drinking black coffee and wrenching away the next day, yelling at the parts guy because the delivery is ten minutes late and I *need* those gaskets right then. And then suddenly my husband is standing in the kitchen telling me it’s the weekend and I need to calm down and stop pacing holes in the rug. But to me, it feels like no time has passed at all, or maybe a hundred years has passed. I just completely lose the thread of it. 

So if you're asking for an exact number of days, like, is it three days or seven days or whatever? I honestly couldn't tell you. It just lasts until it doesn't. Until I finally hit that wall and level out. While it's happening, it’s just this massive blur of being awake and angry and doing a million things at once, and feeling like everyone else is moving in slow motion. I wish I could give you a neat little timeline, but I just... I don't track it. I'm too busy being furious and invincible to look at a clock, you know? It's just a blur until it stops.

inference.note: Patient reports psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions of surveillance) persisting unchanged during both manic-like episodes and euthymic periods, confirming psychosis independent of mood disturbance. The manic episodes (decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, irritability, increased goal-directed activity) without any depressive episodes support the bipolar type of schizoaffective disorder, narrowing from unspecified to F25.0.

doctor.intent: Determine what proportion of the total 10-month illness duration has been spent in these high-energy/irritable mood episodes versus in a normal or depressed mood state, to assess whether mood symptoms have been present for a substantial portion of the illness course (key for schizoaffective vs. primary psychotic disorder distinction)
doctor.question: Looking back over the whole ten months, would you say these high-energy, irritable episodes have taken up most of that time, or have they been relatively brief episodes with longer stretches of your mood being normal in between?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: Most of this past year has been taken over by those high-energy stretches where I talk too fast, take on too much, and feel driven like I can’t slow down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the high-energy, irritable (manic) episodes have taken up the majority of the time over the duration of the illness, which directly corresponds to this additional requirement.

patient.answer:
Oh, definitely most of the time. If I really sit and look back at it... honestly, most of this past year has just been completely taken over by those high-energy stretches. It’s not just a few days here and there, it’s... it's the main thing that’s been happening to me. 

I’ll just be in this state where I talk way too fast—like, my husband will literally have to hold his hands up and tell me to breathe because the words are just tumbling out of my mouth and I can't even stop them. And at the shop, I just take on way too much. I’ll volunteer for the hardest diagnostic jobs, I’ll tell the service advisor to just keep stacking the repair orders on my box, and I’ll have three cars torn apart in my bays at the exact same time. I just feel so incredibly driven, you know? Like there’s this motor inside me that’s redlining and I just can't slow down. 

Even when I know I should take a lunch break, even when my hands are physically cramping from gripping the impact wrench all day, I just keep pushing and pushing. I can't leave a job half-finished, so I just stay under the hood, talking a mile a minute to anyone who walks by. So, yeah, those quiet periods I mentioned before? Where I actually level out and sleep for a normal amount of time? They are definitely the exception. The vast majority of these ten months, it’s just been me running at a million miles an hour, completely taken over by that intense energy, just going and going and going.

inference.note: Patient confirms manic-like episodes (little sleep, grandiosity, irritability, increased goal-directed activity) have occupied the majority of the 10-month illness course, while psychotic symptoms (auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions) persist unchanged even during euthymic periods. This pattern—mood episode present for the majority of the illness duration plus psychosis persisting outside mood episodes—strongly supports schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, and rules out mood disorder with psychotic features or brief psychotic disorder.
